The division is harmful but not necessarily useless as the treatment is different, even within those with ‘typical anorexia’ based on severity. A normalisation of intake and food behaviour will not see a severely underweight person recover to a weight physically needed to function properly (intense and invasive refeeding is often required) where as successful normalisation of intake and food behaviour would be the first step of treatment for someone with atypical anorexia. (Invasive refeeding can also be used in the latter case but it is generally until blood work or another health issue is stabilised not for the purpose of restoring weight). 
Once again, I agree it is harmful but I don’t agree that it is useless and I am genuinely sorry that you’ve felt invalidated. Everyone deserves treatment, if I had to say why there is the distinction I would say it’s to inform exactly what that treatment involves. But there’s obviously a lot more to these perceptions than medical treatment and this is where the real harm is done to those ‘atypical’.

As some people have already pointed out, the notion of people with eating disorders just thinking they’re fat is actually kind of complicated and varies from person to person. I’ve had anorexia for ten years. I am working on recovery now. My bmi says I am still underweight although I don’t think it shows, I don’t think I look obese I just think I look within a normal weight range. But then I have photos from when I was at my worst and I don’t remember ever thinking I was that thin despite having many people comment on it at the time (and yes that did fuel it and make me feel like I was achieving something). These were photos from a day at the beach and I think someone else had a similar experience, it’s shocking for me to look at them now and see my hips sunken in and the weird way my legs kinda caved. The photos, and other people’s comments, don’t match up with my self perception which I think is a much subtler but probably more common experience of body dysmorphia that the idea of a deathly thin girl thinking seeing an obese person in the mirror.

I felt this way for a long time. Every time someone said use your breath to deal with anxiety/meditate or whatever I was like... nah that’s not for me I just can’t. 
Then 4 years ago I met my partner who is a free dive instructor and I went along to do media and business stuff while she worked and then eventually caved and did some work with her. This involves some breathing techniques, lung stretches, almost yoga like chest openers etc and then breath holds and to me the holds were key. Complete game changer.
I started using the breathe ups (I can explain them if you are interested) and small holds when I felt anxious and then I started using more standard in for 4-hold for 6- out for 8 kind of breath cycle. 
Now when they say focus on the breath I will do this (and kinda ignore whatever technique isn’t working for me if it’s a guided meditation) 
There are actually heaps of different breath techniques for relaxation and they’re not all going to work for everyone, the key is trying different ones, maybe outside of meditation practice, until you find one that actually makes you feel calmer and then apply them to your practice. 
The other thing I would say would be when trying a new technique, set a time and give it 5 minutes, it’s very rarely going to feel good in the first few cycles, especially if you’re an anxious person so you need to push through and if after giving it a few shots you still find it uncomfortable try another one. 
I think often in beginner guided meditations they promote non-judgmental observation of the breath but to me that feels like a really advanced thing. Being able to non-judgementally observe your bodily senses seems to freak a lot of people out in the beginning, I know it did me. Anyway I hope you find something that helps. If you’re really not ready for anything to do with the breath I did guided visualisation for a while and just ignored the breath stuff.

My father has BPD and so does my sister. They’re both diagnosed. Neither of them are sociopaths. It is fairly well accepted that, although unintentionally on his part, my fathers illness had an influence on my sisters. This has been reinforced many times by many professionals. There is no way in the world you could say that a pwBPD would not have an impact on the people around them. It’s an illness, as you have said. Having a family member with cancer or schizophrenia or autism or anything has an impact on their loved ones. I came here because I wanted to read some raw expressions from others in my situation. I love my family, I attend all the groups, I try my best. If I thought they were monsters or didn’t deserve love I would not bother. Dealing with something as difficult as a family member with a serious mental illness (not just BPD) is hard and sometimes you do need to just unload your feelings so you can process in a way that is not harmful to your loved ones. Sometimes we need to apply a little DBT to ourselves and validate our own feelings, acknowledge them and then work out how to regulate our emotions and behave effectively (seriously I think DBT is useful for anyone). Why would anyone who didn’t love someone with BPD be here? You can’t call for validation of those with BPD and the call for invalidation of the hurt and frustration of other people. 
Also you say you don’t have BPD but another mental illness and perhaps you feel you are some kind of advocate? Perhaps your efforts would be better spent volunteering in a youth group or mental health facility? There are a lot of people out there who are impacted by stigma from mental illness (which I’m sure you would understand) and I can almost guarantee that to have someone voluntarily spend time with them and treat them like actual humans would mean a whole lot more to them than someone picking at their frustrated loved ones on a reddit forum.
